SOURCE: AWS IAM Access Analyzer Documentation
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/access-analyzer/latest/APIReference/Welcome.html
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-reference-policy-checks.html
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-unused-access-analyzer.html
TYPE: Summary of the cited authoritative AWS pages; paraphrased, not verbatim.

AWS IAM ACCESS ANALYZER — OVERVIEW:
AWS IAM Access Analyzer helps identify resources in your organization and accounts that
are shared with an external entity. It uses automated reasoning (provable security) to
analyze resource-based policies and generate findings when access is granted to external
principals (outside your AWS organization or account).

ANALYSIS TYPES:
1. External Access Analysis: Identifies resources accessible from outside the AWS
   account or organization zone of trust. Supported resource types include: S3 buckets,
   IAM roles (trust policies), KMS keys, Lambda functions, SQS queues, Secrets Manager
   secrets, SNS topics, EBS volume snapshots, RDS snapshots, ECR repositories.
2. Unused Access Analysis: Identifies unused permissions, roles, and access keys.
   Reports IAM roles with permissions unused for a configurable tracking period.
   The tracking-period default is documented on the dedicated Unused Access
   Analyzer page (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-unused-access-analyzer.html);
   this framework does not assert a specific default value here.
3. Policy Validation: Analyzes IAM policy JSON for correctness, best-practice adherence,
   and security warnings before policies are attached (preventive control).
4. Policy Generation: Generates least-privilege IAM policies based on observed CloudTrail
   access activity over a specified period.

RELATIONSHIP TO THIS FRAMEWORK:
- External Access findings complement Phase 1 RBAC checks by identifying cross-account
  role trust exposures (iam_role_cross_account_readonlyaccess_policy rule).
- Unused Access findings align with Phase 1 checks for inactive users/access keys
  (iam_user_accesskey_unused, iam_user_console_access_unused rules).
- Policy Validation output can be incorporated as an authoritative severity signal:
  Access Analyzer policy validation produces ERROR, SECURITY_WARNING, GENERAL_WARNING,
  and SUGGESTION finding categories mapped to specific policy checks (per
  docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-reference-policy-checks.html).
- Access Analyzer does NOT detect privilege escalation paths — this is a differentiated
  capability provided by Phase 2 of this framework.

ACCESS ANALYZER POLICY-CHECK FINDING CATEGORIES (per the policy-checks reference page):
- ERROR: Policy syntax error or invalid reference. Action: fix before deployment.
- SECURITY_WARNING: Grants broader access than intended (e.g., wildcard principal).
- GENERAL_WARNING: Policy may not achieve the intended effect (e.g., redundant Allow).
- SUGGESTION: Minor improvement opportunity (e.g., more specific resource ARN).

RELEVANT IAM ACTIONS:
- access-analyzer:ValidatePolicy — analyze policy JSON before attachment
- access-analyzer:ListFindings — retrieve analyzer findings programmatically
- access-analyzer:CreateAnalyzer — configure a new analyzer for the account or org

SOURCE: AWS CloudTrail Documentation — Log File Integrity Validation and Monitoring
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/monitor-cloudtrail-log-files-with-cloudwatch-logs.html
TYPE: Summary of the cited authoritative AWS pages; paraphrased, not verbatim.

CLOUDTRAIL LOG INTEGRITY — OVERVIEW:
AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation uses SHA-256 hashing and SHA-256 with RSA
for digital signing of digest files. When enabled, CloudTrail creates a digest file for
every hour of log delivery, containing SHA-256 hashes of all log files in that period.
The digest file itself is signed by AWS using a public-private key pair.

INTEGRITY VALIDATION SIGNIFICANCE:
- Tampered log files can be detected because their computed SHA-256 hash will not match
  the hash recorded in the digest file.
- Deleted log files are detected because the digest references them by hash.
- Deleted digest files are detectable via the chain of digest file references.
- This provides cryptographic evidence that CloudTrail records have not been modified or
  deleted after delivery — a critical capability for forensic investigations.

RELEVANT API ACTIONS FOR INTEGRITY:
- cloudtrail:CreateTrail — should require log file validation enabled (EnableLogFileValidation=True)
- cloudtrail:UpdateTrail — can disable log file validation (security regression)
- cloudtrail:DeleteTrail — T1562.001 indicator; eliminates future log delivery
- cloudtrail:StopLogging — suspends logging without deleting the trail

CLOUDTRAIL MONITORING WITH CLOUDWATCH:
CloudTrail can deliver events to CloudWatch Logs for real-time metric filtering and alarms.
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark Recommendation 4.x specifies metric filters and alarms for:
- Unauthorized API calls (ErrorCode = AccessDenied or UnauthorizedAccess)
- Root account usage
- IAM policy changes (eventName starts with Create/Update/Delete* and eventSource=iam.amazonaws.com)
- CloudTrail configuration changes
- S3 bucket policy changes

FRAMEWORK INTEGRATION:
Phase 3 CloudTrail normalizer ingests events from cloudtrail.amazonaws.com. Detection of
DeleteTrail or StopLogging from a principal with a Phase 2 escalation path constitutes a
STRONGLY_CORRELATED alert with MITRE T1562.001 (Defense Evasion). Log integrity enables
forensic confirmation that prior Phase 3 CloudTrail evidence has not been tampered with.

KEY CLOUDTRAIL LIMITATIONS RELEVANT TO FRAMEWORK:
- CloudTrail records management events by default; data events (S3 object access, Lambda
  invocations) require explicit configuration and incur additional cost.
- Lookup Events API has a 90-day lookback limit and is rate-limited (2 requests/second).
- Cross-account trail delivery to a central S3 bucket requires bucket policy allowing
  the source account's CloudTrail service principal.

AWS CloudTrail — LookupEvents and Event History Limits
Source: AWS CloudTrail official documentation
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/APIReference/API_LookupEvents.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/view-cloudtrail-events.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/logging-management-events-with-cloudtrail.html

LookupEvents API:
LookupEvents is an AWS CloudTrail API that can look up management events and CloudTrail Insights events captured by CloudTrail for the past 90 days in a Region.

Lookup characteristics:
- maximum 50 results per response
- pagination via NextToken
- request rate limit of 2 lookup requests per second per account per Region
- LookupAttributes currently support only one attribute per request
- supported management-event lookup attributes include EventId, EventName, EventSource, ReadOnly, ResourceName, ResourceType, Username, and AccessKeyId

Event history:
CloudTrail event history is enabled by default and provides a searchable record of the past 90 days of management events in a single AWS account and Region.

Important limitations of event history:
- shows management events only
- does not show data events, Insights events, or network activity events
- does not provide organization-level aggregation
- is limited to a single account, a single Region, one attribute filter, and a time range

Relationship to this framework:
Phase 3 uses LookupEvents-compatible CloudTrail management-event retrieval as an initial dynamic evidence source. The collector writes raw events to disk, and the normalizer extracts fields needed for IAM correlation.

Framework note:
This framework currently focuses on IAM/STS-relevant management events. Full CloudTrail coverage would require trails or event data stores for broader event types and longer retention.

AWS Cross-Account Policy Evaluation Logic
Type: Direct summary from AWS official documentation
Source: AWS IAM User Guide
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies-cross-account-resource-access.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html

Overview:
When a principal in one AWS account requests access to a resource in another AWS account, AWS performs cross-account policy evaluation. AWS evaluates the request in both the trusted account and the trusting account.

Core rule:
A cross-account request is allowed only if both evaluations return Allow.

Trusted and trusting sides:
- The trusted side is the caller’s account, where identity-based permissions are evaluated.
- The trusting side is the resource owner’s account, where the resource-based policy or role trust policy is evaluated.

Cross-account access requirements:
- A resource-based policy or trust policy in the trusting account must allow the external principal or account.
- An identity-based policy in the trusted account must also allow the calling principal to make the request.
- If either side does not allow the request, the final result is deny.

Role-assumption relevance:
For cross-account AssumeRole access, the target role’s trust policy defines which external principal or account may assume the role, while the external caller still needs permission to call sts:AssumeRole on that role.

Relationship to this framework:
This framework uses cross-account policy evaluation logic to reason about:
- cross-account trust relationships
- role assumption feasibility
- graph edges involving external principals
- CloudTrail events that traverse account boundaries

Framework note:
This file is a retrieval-oriented summary of AWS cross-account logic. The AWS diagrams and examples remain the authoritative reference for exact evaluation behavior.

EC2 Instance Profiles and Role Credentials
Type: Curated synthesis from AWS official documentation
Source: AWS IAM and Amazon EC2 official documentation
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/iam-roles-for-amazon-ec2.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/instance-metadata-security-credentials.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2_instance-profiles.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2.html

Overview:
Applications running on an EC2 instance can use temporary AWS credentials from an IAM role attached to that instance. AWS makes this possible through an instance profile associated with the EC2 instance.

Key points:
- An EC2 instance uses an instance profile to receive an IAM role
- Only one role can be attached to an EC2 instance at a time
- Applications on the instance can obtain temporary credentials from the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS)
- AWS recommends roles and temporary credentials instead of long-term access keys on EC2 instances

Credential retrieval:
AWS documents that applications and tools running on the instance can retrieve temporary credentials from instance metadata. These credentials are automatically rotated by AWS.

Security relevance:
If a principal can influence which role is associated with an EC2 instance, and can also access the instance or workload, that principal may gain the effective permissions of the attached role through the instance environment.

IAM relevance:
Instance profiles are operationally important to IAM security because they connect:
- role attachment
- role passing
- EC2 execution context
- temporary credential availability

Relationship to this framework:
This framework uses EC2 instance-profile and role-credential behavior to explain service-mediated privilege-escalation paths such as PassRole via EC2 and AddRoleToInstanceProfile-driven transitions.

AWS IAM Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) and Tag Security
Type: Direct summary from AWS official documentation with framework-specific security note
Source: AWS IAM official documentation
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction_attribute-based-access-control.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_tags.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_iam-tags.html

Overview:
AWS IAM supports attribute-based access control (ABAC) by using tags attached to principals and resources during authorization. In IAM policies, tag-aware access control commonly uses condition keys such as aws:PrincipalTag, aws:ResourceTag, aws:RequestTag, and aws:TagKeys.

Relevant tag condition logic:
- aws:PrincipalTag/key compares the request against tags attached to the calling IAM user or role
- aws:ResourceTag/key compares the request against tags attached to the target resource
- aws:RequestTag/key controls which tag key-value pairs may be included in a tagging request
- aws:TagKeys controls which tag keys may appear in a request

IAM-specific tag control:
AWS documents that IAM users and roles themselves can be controlled through tag-based conditions. This allows policies to restrict what tagged IAM principals can do and what tag values may be added, changed, or removed on IAM users and roles.

Security note for ABAC environments:
When ABAC is used as an authorization model, the security of the model depends on the integrity of the tags involved in access decisions. If a principal can freely modify authorization-relevant tags on itself or on target resources, the ABAC design may become unsafe. In practice, tagging permissions and tag condition controls should be treated as part of the authorization boundary.

Relationship to this framework:
Phase 1 includes ABAC-oriented checks for risky tag-dependent access configurations. In this framework, IAM tag-modification events such as TagUser, TagRole, UntagUser, and UntagRole are treated as implementation-level signals that may be relevant to privilege escalation or access manipulation in ABAC-governed environments. They should not be presented as direct MITRE procedure examples unless separately supported by MITRE documentation.

AWS IAM Access Analyzer — Policy Validation and Access Findings
Source: AWS IAM official documentation
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-reference-policy-checks.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html

Overview:
AWS IAM Access Analyzer helps identify unintended access and policy issues across AWS environments. Relevant capabilities include:
- policy validation for IAM and resource-based policies
- external access analysis for supported resource types
- unused access analysis for IAM users and roles

Policy validation:
IAM Access Analyzer provides policy checks that identify errors, security warnings, general warnings, and suggestions. These checks help detect malformed or risky policy constructs before or during deployment.

Examples of relevant policy-validation categories:
- missing required elements such as Principal in resource-based policies
- invalid or unsupported actions, resources, or condition usage
- broad or risky policy patterns that may weaken intended access control

External access analysis:
IAM Access Analyzer can generate findings when supported resources are accessible from outside the account or organization. AWS documents IAM roles among the supported resource types for external access analysis.

Unused access analysis:
IAM Access Analyzer can generate findings for unused IAM roles, unused access keys, unused passwords, and unused services or actions associated with active IAM identities.

Relationship to this framework:
Phase 1 uses rule-based checks that are conceptually related to the kinds of issues IAM Access Analyzer can surface, especially around overly broad access, risky trust relationships, and policy quality. However, Phase 1 uses framework-specific logic and should not be described as a direct wrapper around the Access Analyzer API.

AWS IAM and STS Condition Keys and Request Context
Type: Curated synthesis from AWS official documentation
Source: AWS IAM User Guide
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_iam-condition-keys.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.html

Overview:
AWS policy conditions are evaluated against the request context. A Condition element can compare request attributes against global condition keys or service-specific condition keys.

Condition-key categories:
- Global condition keys use the aws: prefix.
- Service-specific condition keys use a service prefix such as iam: or sts:.
- IAM and AWS STS also support IAM-specific and STS-relevant condition context keys for trust, tagging, and identity controls.

Examples relevant to IAM security:
- aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent can be used to require MFA context
- aws:PrincipalOrgID can restrict access to principals in a specific AWS Organization
- aws:SourceAccount can help limit service-to-service confused-deputy exposure in supported patterns
- sts:ExternalId is used in third-party cross-account role assumption scenarios
- aws:ResourceTag and iam:ResourceTag can be used in tag-aware authorization logic

ABAC relevance:
Tag-aware authorization can use aws:PrincipalTag, aws:ResourceTag, aws:RequestTag, and aws:TagKeys. These keys are important when access decisions depend on tags attached to principals or resources.

Trust-policy relevance:
Condition keys are often critical in role trust policies. Even when a principal is listed in the Principal element, conditions may still be required to limit assumption to expected callers, organizations, or MFA-authenticated sessions.

Relationship to this framework:
This framework uses condition-key and request-context logic to interpret:
- Phase 1 ABAC and trust-policy checks
- Phase 2 edge feasibility and conditional transitions
- Phase 3 explanation of why a role assumption or tag-sensitive action may be risky or constrained

Framework note:
This file is a curated AWS-only synthesis because request context, IAM condition keys, STS trust constraints, and confused-deputy protections are documented across multiple official pages rather than one single page.

AWS IAM PassRole — Service Role Delegation
Source: AWS IAM User Guide — Grant a user permissions to pass a role to an AWS service
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_passrole.html

Overview:
iam:PassRole is an IAM permission that controls whether a principal can pass an IAM role to an AWS service. It is not a standalone service API call; instead, AWS checks this permission when a request includes a role parameter for a service resource.

Key constraints:
- A role can be passed only to a service in the same AWS account
- The role’s trust policy must allow the target service principal
- The iam:PassedToService condition key can be used to restrict which service may receive the role

Operational security relevance:
A principal with iam:PassRole on a powerful role, combined with permission to create or configure a service resource that accepts that role, may indirectly obtain the effective privileges of that role through the service.

Examples:
- EC2 launch paths where a role is associated with an instance profile
- Lambda creation or update paths where a function is configured to run with a role
- Other service-role delegation paths where the service later acts using the role’s permissions

AddRoleToInstanceProfile:
iam:AddRoleToInstanceProfile is operationally relevant because it can associate a role with an EC2 instance profile, enabling the instance to use that role’s credentials.

Relationship to this framework:
Phase 2 models PassRole-based privilege escalation as researcher-defined edge patterns such as service-mediated privilege transitions. These edges depend on both role-passing capability and the service role trust relationship.

Framework note:
This file is retrieval-oriented AWS documentation summary. Service-specific exploitation chains are framework-level analysis logic, not direct AWS claims of privilege escalation.

AWS IAM Policy Evaluation Logic
Source: AWS IAM User Guide — Policy evaluation logic
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-basics.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account.html

Overview:
When a principal makes a request to AWS, AWS authenticates the principal if required, builds the request context, determines which policy types apply, and then evaluates those applicable policies to decide whether the request is allowed or denied.

Core evaluation principles:
- AWS uses explicit deny logic. If an applicable policy explicitly denies the request, that deny overrides any allow.
- If no applicable policy allows the request, the request is denied by default.
- In same-account scenarios, identity-based and resource-based policies can combine, and the resulting permissions depend on the applicable policy types.
- Permissions boundaries restrict identity-based permissions by intersection.
- AWS Organizations SCPs and RCPs can further restrict effective permissions.

Same-account evaluation:
AWS provides separate evaluation flow charts for IAM users and IAM roles within a single account. These flows should be treated as the authoritative reference for detailed same-account policy reasoning.

Cross-account evaluation:
AWS evaluates cross-account access using a separate logic model. In general, the trusted side must allow access through a resource-based policy (or role trust policy for role assumption), and the calling side must also have an identity-based permission that authorizes the request.

Trust policy note:
A role trust policy is a resource-based policy attached to an IAM role. It controls who can call AssumeRole or related STS operations against that role, while the role’s permissions policy controls what the resulting role session can do after assumption.

Relationship to this framework:
This framework uses AWS policy evaluation logic as background knowledge for:
- Phase 1 interpretation of IAM misconfigurations
- Phase 2 construction of permission-transition edges
- Phase 3 explanation and grounding of correlated identity events

Framework note:
Detailed same-account and cross-account reasoning should be retrieved from their dedicated AWS KB files rather than relying only on this overview.

SOURCE: AWS Organizations Documentation — Service Control Policies (SCPs)
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html
TYPE: Summary of the cited authoritative AWS pages; paraphrased, not verbatim.

SERVICE CONTROL POLICIES (SCPs) — OVERVIEW:
Service Control Policies are a type of organization policy that you can use to manage
permissions in your organization. SCPs offer central control over the maximum available
permissions for all accounts in your organization.

KEY EVALUATION RULES:
1. SCPs do not grant permissions. They define the maximum permissions that identity-based
   policies can grant to IAM principals (users and roles) in member accounts.
2. An effective permission requires BOTH: (a) SCP Allow (or no SCP deny in deny-list strategy),
   AND (b) IAM identity-based policy Allow.
3. An explicit SCP Deny overrides any IAM Allow — it is always effective regardless of what
   IAM identity policies permit.
4. The management account of an organization is NOT restricted by SCPs. SCPs apply only
   to member accounts.
5. Service-linked roles are exempt from SCP restrictions.

SCP STRATEGY TYPES:
- Deny-list strategy (default with FullAWSAccess): All actions allowed unless explicitly
  denied by a custom SCP. FullAWSAccess is a managed SCP allowing all actions. Custom SCPs
  add specific denies on top.
- Allow-list strategy: FullAWSAccess is removed; only explicitly allowed actions are
  permitted. Less common, more restrictive, more complex to manage.

SCPS AND PRIVILEGE ESCALATION PATHS:
In the context of IAM privilege escalation analysis:
- An SCP denying iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy, or iam:CreatePolicyVersion
  organization-wide eliminates entire classes of escalation paths, even if the IAM
  identity policy permits them.
- SCPs denying sts:AssumeRole for certain conditions can block lateral movement paths.
- SCP protection is a defense-in-depth control: it does not replace IAM least privilege
  but provides an additional boundary.
- Removing an SCP would immediately reactivate all previously blocked escalation paths.

FRAMEWORK INTEGRATION:
Phase 2 of this framework applies SCP-aware filtering via scp_filter.py after BFS
path discovery. Paths blocked by SCPs are annotated as scp_blocked=True (latent risk)
rather than removed, reflecting that the IAM misconfiguration persists even when an SCP
provides temporary mitigation. This distinction is critical for risk management.

IMPORTANT LIMITATIONS:
- SCPs do not restrict the AWS account root user.
- SCPs cannot be applied to the management account.
- Resource-based policies are not controlled by SCPs.
- Permissions boundaries are separate from SCPs (both can restrict actions independently).

AWS Policy Evaluation for Requests Within a Single Account
Type: Direct summary from AWS official documentation
Source: AWS IAM User Guide
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-basics.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html

Overview:
For requests within a single AWS account, AWS evaluates the policies that apply to the request context and then decides whether the request is allowed or denied. AWS uses explicit deny logic and default deny logic.

Core rules:
- If any applicable policy explicitly denies the request, AWS denies the request.
- If no applicable policy allows the request, AWS denies the request by default.
- Identity-based policies and resource-based policies can both contribute to an allow decision in same-account scenarios.
- Permissions boundaries restrict identity-based permissions by intersection.
- AWS Organizations SCPs and RCPs can further restrict effective permissions.

Same-account reasoning:
AWS provides separate evaluation paths for IAM users and IAM roles. In same-account scenarios, the final result depends on the applicable policy types and whether any explicit deny overrides the request.

Trust policy note:
For IAM roles, the trust policy is a resource-based policy that controls who may call AssumeRole or related STS operations against the role. The role permissions policy separately controls what the resulting role session can do after assumption.

Relationship to this framework:
This framework uses same-account policy evaluation logic to interpret:
- Phase 1 IAM misconfiguration findings
- Phase 2 permission-transition feasibility
- Phase 3 explanation of correlated access events

Framework note:
This file is a retrieval-oriented summary. AWS policy evaluation diagrams and examples remain the authoritative reference for edge cases.

AWS STS AssumeRole and Trust Policy Evaluation
Source: AWS IAM and AWS STS official documentation
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRole.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_iam-condition-keys.html

AssumeRole overview:
sts:AssumeRole is an AWS STS API operation that returns temporary security credentials for an IAM role. To assume a role, the caller must be trusted by the role’s trust policy, and in many scenarios the caller also needs an identity-based policy that allows sts:AssumeRole on the target role.

Trust policy structure:
A trust policy is a required resource-based policy attached to an IAM role. It specifies which principals are trusted to assume the role. AWS documents that principals in a role trust policy can include AWS accounts, IAM users, IAM roles, federated principals, and AWS services.

Useful trust-policy conditions:
Commonly used condition keys in trust policies include:
- aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent
- aws:PrincipalOrgID
- sts:ExternalId
Additional IAM and STS condition keys can be used depending on the trust model.

Broad trust risks:
A trust policy can become overly broad if it trusts an entire external account or uses a very broad principal scope without restrictive conditions. AWS also documents that wildcard use in the Principal element has important limitations and risks, and recommends narrowing access with conditions where broader trust is unavoidable.

Cross-account trust:
For cross-account role assumption, the trusting account uses the role’s trust policy to specify the trusted account or principal, and the trusted side must also grant the caller permission to call sts:AssumeRole. Both sides matter.

Role chaining:
A role session can assume another role if the session has permission to do so and the target role’s trust policy allows it. This is operationally relevant to multi-hop access paths.

UpdateAssumeRolePolicy:
iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy replaces the trust policy attached to a role. In security analysis, this is a high-impact action because a principal that can modify trust policy can potentially expand who is allowed to assume the role.

Relationship to this framework:
This framework uses trust-policy and AssumeRole logic in:
- Phase 2, to determine whether an AssumeRole edge is reachable
- Phase 3, to interpret CloudTrail role-assumption events and trust-policy modification events

Framework note:
This file is retrieval-oriented explanatory material based on AWS documentation. It should not be treated as a formal proof model of all IAM edge cases; the AWS documentation pages remain the primary authority.

CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark — IAM Controls (Public Partial Reference)
Type: Public-summary note based on official CIS and AWS Security Hub public pages
Source: CIS official benchmark page
URL: https://www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/amazon_web_services
Source: AWS Security Hub — CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/cis-aws-foundations-benchmark.html
Source: AWS Security Hub control reference
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/securityhub-controls-reference.html

Important scope note:
This file is intentionally limited to publicly accessible material.
- CIS states that the AWS Benchmark PDF is freely available for non-commercial use from the official CIS site.
- This file does not reproduce benchmark text from the PDF.
- Instead, it records public benchmark availability and publicly visible AWS Security Hub CIS benchmark control coverage.
- Exact benchmark-version citations should be verified manually against the downloaded CIS PDF or the AWS Security Hub control reference before use in a research paper.

Publicly visible IAM-related CIS benchmark coverage in AWS Security Hub:
AWS Security Hub publicly lists IAM-focused controls within the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark standard, including controls such as:
- IAM policies should not allow full "*" administrative privileges
- IAM users should not have IAM policies attached
- IAM users' access keys should be rotated every 90 days or less
- IAM root user access key should not exist
- MFA should be enabled for IAM users that have a console password
- Hardware MFA should be enabled for the root user
- MFA should be enabled for the root user
- IAM password policy should require minimum password length of 14 or greater
- IAM password policy should prevent password reuse

How to use this file safely:
- Use it as a public benchmark-alignment note, not as a substitute for the full CIS benchmark text
- Do not quote proprietary or undisplayed CIS wording from this file
- Before citing a specific CIS benchmark version or control number in a paper, verify it directly against the downloaded CIS benchmark PDF or the AWS Security Hub control reference page

Relationship to this framework:
Phase 1 contains IAM checks whose security intent overlaps with publicly visible AWS Security Hub CIS benchmark control topics. Any paper claim about CIS alignment should be phrased carefully and verified against the exact benchmark version used.

SOURCE: AWS Security Documentation — Emergency Access Procedures
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_temp_control-access_disable-perms.html
REFERENCE: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-use-aws-iam-to-manage-emergency-access/
NOTE: Curated synthesis of AWS security blog content and IAM documentation. Labeled as synthesis.

BREAK-GLASS ACCESS IN AWS — OVERVIEW:
Break-glass (emergency access) procedures define how privileged access is obtained in
crisis situations when normal access pathways are unavailable. In AWS environments,
break-glass accounts or roles are pre-provisioned with elevated permissions but kept
isolated from routine use. Their use should be detectable, auditable, and revocable.

STANDARD BREAK-GLASS ARCHITECTURE:
1. Dedicated Break-Glass IAM Role: A role with elevated permissions (e.g., Administrator
   access) that is normally inaccessible. Trust policy restricts AssumeRole to specific
   principals with MFA required (Condition: {"Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}}).
2. Break-Glass User Account: A separate IAM user with no permissions except sts:AssumeRole
   on the break-glass role. Credentials are stored in a physical safe or offline vault.
3. CloudWatch Alarm on Usage: A CloudWatch metric filter monitors CloudTrail for
   AssumeRole calls on the break-glass role ARN. Any usage triggers immediate alerting.
4. Session Duration Limit: MaxSessionDuration on the break-glass role is set to 1 hour
   (minimum needed for the emergency task), not the default 12 hours.
5. Post-Use Review: All actions taken during break-glass sessions must be reviewed via
   CloudTrail within 24 hours. The break-glass role's access keys are rotated afterward.

RELATIONSHIP TO FRAMEWORK FINDINGS:
Phase 3 alerts involving the break-glass role ARN should be treated specially:
- A STRONGLY_CORRELATED alert on a break-glass role assumption may be legitimate (authorized)
  or malicious (stolen break-glass credentials). Context is critical.
- Phase 1 findings on break-glass roles (e.g., missing MFA condition) represent HIGH severity
  because they eliminate the primary control distinguishing authorized from unauthorized use.
- Phase 2 paths through break-glass roles to admin principals are expected by design, but
  should still be reported so that trust policy conditions (MFA requirement) are verified.

REMEDIATION GUIDANCE FOR BREAK-GLASS ROLE FINDINGS:
- Add Condition: {"Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}} to break-glass trust policy
- Set MaxSessionDuration to 3600 (one hour) on break-glass roles
- Apply tagging: aws:RequestTag/Purpose=BreakGlass for ABAC tracking
- Enable CloudTrail data events for the break-glass role ARN specifically
- Review break-glass role usage in CloudTrail at minimum monthly (AWS Config rule)

FALSE POSITIVE CONSIDERATION FOR PHASE 3:
When evaluating alerts involving known break-glass role ARNs, the LLM false_positive_assessment
should note that usage during a declared incident may be authorized. Cross-reference with
incident management system timestamps if available.

SOURCE: AWS IAM Best Practices Documentation + AWS Well-Architected Framework (Security Pillar)
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html
REFERENCE: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/security-pillar/identity-and-access-management.html
NOTE: Curated synthesis of AWS IAM best practices documentation and Well-Architected Security Pillar guidance.

LEAST PRIVILEGE PRINCIPLE IN AWS IAM:
Least privilege means granting only the permissions required to perform a task, nothing more.
AWS IAM best practices define the following patterns for achieving least privilege:

PATTERN 1 — TASK-BASED ROLES:
Create IAM roles scoped to a single workload task. Avoid reusing roles across services.
A Lambda function that reads from DynamoDB should have only dynamodb:GetItem and
dynamodb:Query on the specific table ARN — not dynamodb:* on *.

PATTERN 2 — RESOURCE-LEVEL PERMISSIONS:
Always specify the resource ARN rather than wildcard (*) when AWS supports resource-level
permissions. Most IAM actions support resource-level ARN specification.
Example: iam:PassRole restricted to arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/specific-role-name.
Wildcard on iam:PassRole (* resource) is a common privilege escalation enabler.

PATTERN 3 — CONDITION-BASED RESTRICTIONS:
Use IAM condition keys to further restrict permission scope:
- aws:RequestedRegion — restrict actions to specific regions
- aws:PrincipalTag — require specific resource tags (ABAC)
- iam:PassedToService — restrict PassRole to a specific AWS service
- aws:SourceIp — restrict API calls to corporate IP ranges

PATTERN 4 — PERMISSION BOUNDARIES:
Permission boundaries define the maximum permissions an IAM entity can have, regardless
of what identity-based policies allow. Use boundaries on delegated role creation to
prevent privilege escalation via role creation.

PATTERN 5 — SENSITIVE ACTION SEPARATION:
Never combine sensitive IAM write permissions with data access in a single role:
- iam:CreatePolicyVersion + s3:GetObject in a single role is a high-risk combination
- Separate IAM administrative roles from workload data-access roles
- Use separate roles for CI/CD deployment vs. runtime workload execution

PATTERN 6 — ACCESS ANALYZER FOR VALIDATION:
Before deploying any IAM policy:
1. Run aws accessanalyzer validate-policy to check for SECURITY_WARNING or ERROR findings
2. Use Policy Simulator to test permission boundaries
3. Use IAM Policy Generation from CloudTrail to baseline minimum required permissions

FRAMEWORK RELEVANCE:
Phase 1 RBAC rules directly test violations of these patterns:
- iam_policy_allows_privilege_escalation: detects dangerous action combinations
- iam_customer_attached_policy_no_administrative_privileges: enforces Pattern 1/5
- iam_no_custom_policy_permissive_role_assumption: enforces Pattern 2 on iam:PassRole
- ABAC rules enforce Pattern 3 (tag-based conditions)
Phase 3 LLM remediation steps should reference these patterns by name when generating
grounded remediation guidance.

Technique: T1070 — Indicator Removal
Tactic: Defense Evasion

Source: MITRE ATT&CK
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1070/

Description:
Adversaries may delete or modify artifacts generated within systems to remove evidence of their presence or hinder defenses. MITRE describes this technique broadly as removing indicators that would otherwise support detection, forensic analysis, or incident response.

AWS-relevant interpretation for this framework:
- DeleteUser may remove an attacker-created IAM user used for persistence
- DeleteRole may remove a role created or altered during escalation activity
- DeleteAccessKey may remove credentials created during adversary activity

Framework note:
These AWS IAM actions are framework-relevant interpretations for cloud identity investigations. They should not be presented as direct MITRE AWS procedure examples from the T1070 page.

Technique: T1078.004 — Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts
Tactics: Defense Evasion, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Initial Access
Platforms: IaaS, Identity Provider, Office Suite, SaaS

Source: MITRE ATT&CK
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/

Description:
Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of cloud accounts to bypass access controls and perform actions associated with initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion. Cloud accounts may be cloud-only or hybrid/federated with on-premises identity systems, which can allow adversaries to affect both cloud and on-premises environments.

MITRE notes that compromised cloud accounts may be used to create Additional Cloud Credentials or to assume Temporary Elevated Cloud Access when role assignments or role assumption policies are misconfigured. Over-privileged cloud accounts may also be used to access sensitive data through cloud APIs.

Detection:
MITRE’s detection strategy emphasizes anomalous authentication and account-usage patterns, such as sign-ins from unusual locations, usage that exceeds the normal scope of the account, or API activity inconsistent with the account’s historical behavior.

Mitigation:
MITRE mitigation guidance includes:
- requiring multi-factor authentication for cloud accounts, especially privileged accounts
- enforcing strong password and access key rotation policies
- routinely reviewing privileged cloud account permission levels
- periodically reviewing user accounts and removing inactive or unnecessary accounts

Framework note:
The # actions metadata line is framework retrieval metadata used by this project’s KB builder. In this framework, CreateLoginProfile and UpdateLoginProfile may be analyzed as implementation-level signals associated with cloud-account abuse, but they should not be presented as direct MITRE AWS procedure examples unless explicitly stated on the MITRE page.

Technique: T1087.004 — Account Discovery: Cloud Account
Tactic: Discovery
Platforms: IaaS, SaaS

Source: MITRE ATT&CK
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087/004/

Description:
Adversaries may attempt to enumerate cloud accounts to understand the identity structure of a target environment. MITRE notes that cloud APIs may be used to retrieve information about accounts, users, roles, and credentials in order to identify valuable targets and understand account posture.

AWS examples cited by MITRE on the T1087.004 technique page:
- aws iam list-users
- aws iam list-roles

Framework-curated AWS interpretation (NOT cited on the MITRE page):
- GenerateCredentialReport, GetCredentialReport are framework-selected
  credential-enumeration actions treated by this project as signals under
  T1087.004 because they return principal and credential inventory. These
  actions are NOT listed as MITRE-cited examples on the T1087.004 page; any
  paper reference must present them as framework-curated, not MITRE-supported.

Detection:
Cloud account discovery may be visible through IAM and identity enumeration activity, especially when credential reporting or identity inventory actions are performed by principals that do not normally require them.

Mitigation:
Defensive value comes from restricting unnecessary identity enumeration permissions and monitoring unusual use of account inventory or credential-reporting capabilities.

Technique: T1098.001 — Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials
Tactics: Persistence, Privilege Escalation
Platforms: IaaS, Identity Provider, SaaS

Source: MITRE ATT&CK
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/001/

Description:
Adversaries may add adversary-controlled credentials to a cloud account to maintain persistent access to victim accounts and instances within the environment. In AWS, MITRE notes examples such as using CreateAccessKey to add access keys to an account, CreateLoginProfile to add a console password, and sts:GetFederationToken to create temporary credentials tied to the original user account. In IaaS contexts, MITRE also notes CreateKeyPair and ImportKeyPair for persistent access to instances.

AWS procedure examples noted by MITRE:
- CreateAccessKey to add access keys to an account
- CreateLoginProfile to add a console password
- sts:GetFederationToken to create temporary credentials
- CreateKeyPair / ImportKeyPair for instance access in IaaS contexts

Detection:
MITRE’s detection strategy focuses on addition of credentials to existing cloud accounts via portal or API by non-standard identities or IP ranges, and on cloud API usage such as CreateAccessKey, ImportKeyPair, or CreateLoginProfile from unusual principals or non-console access patterns.

Mitigation:
MITRE mitigation guidance includes using multi-factor authentication for user and privileged accounts, ensuring low-privileged users cannot add access keys to accounts, and prohibiting sts:GetFederationToken unless explicitly required.

Framework note:
In this framework, AWS IAM / STS events aligned with T1098.001 may be used as retrieval and correlation evidence in Phase 3. Any final alert prioritization remains framework-specific and is not a MITRE severity claim.

Technique: T1098.003 — Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles
Tactics: Persistence, Privilege Escalation
Platforms: IaaS, Identity Provider, Office Suite, SaaS

Source: MITRE ATT&CK
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/003/

Description:
Adversaries may add additional roles or permissions to an adversary-controlled cloud account to maintain persistent access to a tenant. This account modification may follow account creation or other malicious account activity, and may also involve modifying existing valid accounts that the adversary has already compromised.

AWS examples explicitly noted by MITRE:
- CreatePolicyVersion to define a new version of an IAM policy
- AttachUserPolicy to attach an IAM policy with additional or distinct permissions to a compromised user account

Detection:
MITRE’s detection guidance focuses on identifying new IAM roles or policies attached to a user or service outside normal patterns or hours, and on behavioral chains in which a user is granted elevated privileges or roles following suspicious login or account creation activity.

Mitigation:
MITRE mitigation guidance includes:
- using multi-factor authentication for user and privileged accounts
- ensuring that all accounts use the least privileges they require
- ensuring that low-privileged accounts do not have permissions to add permissions to accounts or update IAM policies

Framework note:
In this framework, additional IAM policy- and role-manipulation actions may also be analyzed in Phase 2 and Phase 3 as researcher-defined implementation mappings. Those broader action mappings should not be presented as if they were all explicitly enumerated by MITRE under this technique.

Technique: T1136.003 — Create Account: Cloud Account
Tactic: Persistence
Platforms: IaaS, Identity Provider, Office Suite, SaaS

Source: MITRE ATT&CK
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136/003/

Description:
Adversaries may create a cloud account to maintain access to victim systems. With a sufficient level of access, such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that does not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system.

MITRE notes that cloud accounts can include both user accounts and service-associated accounts, depending on how the cloud provider models identity. MITRE also notes that AWS resources can be granted permission to assume roles.

AWS reference on the MITRE T1136.003 page:
- CreateUser appears in MITRE's T1136.003 detection analytics block as a
  CloudTrail event to monitor for new IAM account creation. CreateUser is
  NOT cited as an adversary procedure example in the technique narrative
  itself — it appears only in the detection analytics. Treat it as a
  MITRE-listed detection signal, not as a MITRE-cited adversary procedure.

Detection:
MITRE’s detection strategy highlights cloud account creation through API, CLI, or console activity, especially when CreateUser events are followed by policy attachment or credential generation. Such sequences are higher-value signals than isolated account creation alone.

Mitigation:
MITRE mitigation guidance includes using multi-factor authentication for user and privileged accounts and limiting the number of identities that can create other accounts. Privileged account creation rights should be tightly restricted.

Framework note:
In this framework, some additional IAM actions such as CreateRole may be analyzed as implementation-level signals related to cloud identity persistence. However, those broader mappings should not be presented as direct MITRE procedure examples unless explicitly supported by the MITRE technique page.

SOURCE: MITRE ATT&CK® for Enterprise (Cloud) — Technique T1530
TECHNIQUE: Data from Cloud Storage
TACTIC: Collection
ATT&CK ID: T1530
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1530/
NOTE: Curated synthesis of MITRE ATT&CK wiki content and AWS S3/IAM documentation.

DESCRIPTION:
Adversaries may access data objects from improperly secured cloud storage. In AWS
contexts, one common manifestation is unauthorized S3 bucket access following IAM
privilege escalation. An adversary with acquired IAM credentials or roles may
enumerate and exfiltrate objects from S3 buckets containing sensitive data
(credentials, backups, source code, PII). The framing above is a framework-level
interpretation of T1530 applied to AWS; MITRE's technique page is tactic-scoped
(Collection) and does not single out S3 as a primary manifestation.

RELEVANT AWS API ACTIONS (IAM-linked):
- s3:GetObject — retrieve individual objects from S3 buckets
- s3:ListBucket — enumerate object keys (prerequisite for bulk collection)
- s3:GetBucketPolicy — read bucket policy to understand access controls
- s3:CopyObject — duplicate objects to attacker-controlled buckets
- sts:AssumeRole — assume a role with S3 read access after IAM escalation

IAM-SPECIFIC RELEVANCE:
This technique typically follows IAM privilege escalation (T1098 or T1078.004). An
adversary who escalates to a role with S3 data access can immediately begin collection.
Relevant IAM misconfigurations that enable this technique:
- Roles with s3:GetObject on * attached (overly permissive S3 data policies)
- Cross-account role trust policies without ExternalId condition (enables collection by third parties)
- Instance profiles with data access attached to publicly accessible EC2 instances

DETECTION IN THIS FRAMEWORK:
Phase 3 correlates S3 API calls against principals that appear in Phase 2 escalation
paths. A principal with a known privilege escalation path who subsequently calls
s3:GetObject or s3:ListBucket represents a potential post-escalation collection event.
CloudTrail event source s3.amazonaws.com is normalized by the CloudTrail normalizer.

REMEDIATION POINTERS:
- Apply S3 bucket policies restricting access to specific roles/VPC endpoints
- Enable S3 server access logging and S3 object-level CloudTrail logging
- Use AWS Macie to classify and alert on sensitive S3 data access
- Enforce s3:GetObject deny in SCPs for non-data-access roles
- Apply aws:PrincipalTag conditions to limit S3 access by environment tag

Technique: T1550.001 — Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
Tactics: Defense Evasion, Lateral Movement
Platforms: Containers, IaaS, Identity Provider, Office Suite, SaaS

Source: MITRE ATT&CK
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/001/

Description:
Adversaries may use stolen application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems. These tokens are commonly used to make authorized API requests on behalf of a user or service, especially in cloud and SaaS environments.

MITRE notes that in AWS and GCP environments, adversaries can request a short-lived access token with the privileges of another user account. In AWS, MITRE specifically notes that an adversary who compromises a user’s AWS API credentials may use sts:GetFederationToken to create a federated user session that has the same permissions as the original user and may persist even if the original user credentials are deactivated.

Detection:
MITRE’s detection strategy includes monitoring the use of AWS STS or similar APIs to request temporary tokens or federation sessions in ways that are inconsistent with normal account activity, such as requests from unexpected principals or regions.

Mitigation:
MITRE mitigation guidance includes:
- restricting use of access tokens outside expected contexts
- auditing cloud accounts and their permissions
- disabling the ability to request temporary account tokens on behalf of other accounts where possible

Framework note:
The # actions metadata line is framework retrieval metadata used by this project’s KB builder. In this framework, broader STS role-assumption actions such as AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithSAML, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, and GetSessionToken may also be retrieved and analyzed because they are operationally relevant to cloud token abuse and temporary credential use. However, they should not all be presented as explicit MITRE AWS procedure examples unless directly supported by the MITRE technique page.

SOURCE: MITRE ATT&CK® for Enterprise (Cloud) — Technique T1552.001
TECHNIQUE: Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
TACTIC: Credential Access
ATT&CK ID: T1552.001
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
NOTE: Curated synthesis of MITRE ATT&CK wiki content and AWS IAM/EC2 metadata documentation.

DESCRIPTION:
Adversaries may search the file system and file contents for insecurely stored credentials.
In AWS environments, this includes access keys stored in EC2 instance user data, hardcoded
credentials in Lambda environment variables, credentials in S3 object contents, IAM
credentials cached in ~/.aws/credentials on EC2 instances, and instance metadata service
(IMDS) token exposure.

RELEVANT AWS EXPOSURE VECTORS:
- EC2 instance user data (ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute) — sometimes contains plaintext credentials
- Lambda environment variables (lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration) — may contain API keys
- SSM Parameter Store (ssm:GetParameter) — may contain secrets if not using SecureString type
- Secrets Manager (secretsmanager:GetSecretValue) — legitimate secrets store (monitor access)
- S3 object contents with access keys (s3:GetObject on credential files)
- EC2 Instance Metadata Service v1 (IMDSv1) — no token required, exploitable via SSRF

IAM-SPECIFIC RELEVANCE:
From an IAM perspective, this technique intersects with:
- Roles with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration on * (enables reading env vars for all functions)
- Roles with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute (enables reading instance user-data)
- Overly permissive SSM parameter read access (ssm:GetParameter on *)
- IMDSv1 enabled on EC2 instances (allows credential theft via SSRF without IAM permission)

EC2 IMDSv2 (token-required mode) mitigates SSRF-based credential theft. IMDSv1 without
PUT token requirement remains a critical IAM exposure risk for workload roles.

DETECTION IN THIS FRAMEWORK:
Phase 3 correlates lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration and ssm:GetParameter calls against
principals with Phase 2 escalation paths. Principals performing broad enumeration of
Lambda environment variables or SSM parameters after obtaining elevated credentials
indicate post-escalation credential harvesting activity.

REMEDIATION POINTERS:
- Enforce IMDSv2 on all EC2 instances. Set the EC2 instance metadata option
  HttpTokens=required via the ec2:ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions API, and
  optionally restrict non-required values using the ec2:MetadataHttpTokens
  IAM condition key (service prefix ec2:, not aws:).
- Never store credentials in Lambda environment variables; use Secrets Manager
- Apply SCP denying ec2:ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions to prevent downgrade to IMDSv1
- Restrict ssm:GetParameter to specific parameter paths using resource conditions
- Enable Secrets Manager rotation and access logging

Technique: T1556.006 — Modify Authentication Process: Multi-Factor Authentication
Tactics: Credential Access, Defense Evasion, Persistence
Platforms: IaaS, Identity Provider, Linux, Office Suite, SaaS, Windows, macOS

Source: MITRE ATT&CK
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/006/

Description:
Adversaries may disable or modify multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms to enable persistent access to compromised accounts. MITRE notes that adversaries may disable MFA defenses, register adversary-controlled MFA methods, or weaken MFA enforcement to allow successful authentication without the expected second factor.

AWS-relevant interpretation for this framework:
- DeactivateMFADevice may indicate disabling MFA protection on an IAM user
- DeleteVirtualMFADevice may indicate removal of a virtual MFA device associated with account protection

Detection:
MITRE detection guidance focuses on suspicious MFA method changes, removal of MFA enforcement, registration of new MFA factors by anomalous users, or successful authentications that occur without expected MFA prompts.

Mitigation:
MITRE mitigation guidance includes reviewing MFA actions alongside authentication logs, ensuring accounts have MFA enabled, enforcing secure enrollment and deactivation procedures, and preferring fail-closed behavior where possible.

Framework note:
The # actions metadata line is framework retrieval metadata. Additional federation-related changes may be operationally relevant to this project, but they should not be presented as explicit MITRE AWS procedure examples for T1556.006 unless directly supported by the MITRE technique page.

SOURCE: MITRE ATT&CK® for Enterprise — Technique T1562.001
TECHNIQUE: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
TACTIC: Defense Evasion
ATT&CK ID: T1562.001
PLATFORMS (per MITRE): Containers, IaaS, Linux, Network Devices, Windows, macOS
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001/
TYPE: Curated synthesis of MITRE ATT&CK technique content and AWS CloudTrail/Config/GuardDuty documentation.

DESCRIPTION:
Adversaries may modify or disable security tools to avoid possible detection of their
malware/tools and activities. In AWS cloud environments, this technique is observed as
unauthorized modification or deletion of CloudTrail trails, disabling AWS Config rules,
stopping GuardDuty detectors, or removing log delivery configurations.

RELEVANT AWS API ACTIONS:
- cloudtrail:DeleteTrail — permanently removes a CloudTrail trail, eliminating audit logs
- cloudtrail:StopLogging — suspends log delivery without removing the trail configuration
- cloudtrail:UpdateTrail — modifies trail settings (e.g., disabling log file validation)
- guardduty:DeleteDetector — removes a GuardDuty detector for an account or region
- guardduty:DisassociateMembers — removes member accounts from GuardDuty monitoring scope
- config:DeleteConfigurationRecorder — stops AWS Config from recording resource changes
- config:StopConfigurationRecorder — pauses Config recording without deleting the recorder
- config:DeleteDeliveryChannel — removes the S3/SNS delivery channel for Config snapshots

IAM-SPECIFIC RELEVANCE:
An adversary who has obtained privileges via IAM privilege escalation (T1078.004 or T1098)
may subsequently impair defenses to conceal ongoing access. Key indicators are:
- CloudTrail deletion/modification following recent IAM permission changes
- GuardDuty detector deletion by a newly privileged principal
- Sequential pattern: IAM escalation → trail deletion (two-step concealment)

DETECTION IN THIS FRAMEWORK:
Phase 3 CloudTrail normalizer ingests cloudtrail.amazonaws.com and guardduty.amazonaws.com
event sources. DeleteTrail, StopLogging, DeleteDetector, and StopConfigurationRecorder
are in the MITRE_SENSITIVE_ACTIONS catalog under Defense Evasion tactic (event_sensitivity=MEDIUM).
STRONGLY_CORRELATED alerts combining a prior Phase 2 escalation path with these events
should be treated as HIGH confidence indicators of active exploitation.

REMEDIATION POINTERS:
- Enable CloudTrail log file integrity validation (SHA-256 hash chaining)
- Apply SCP deny on cloudtrail:DeleteTrail and cloudtrail:StopLogging org-wide
- Configure CloudWatch alarms on CloudTrail API errors and deletion events
- Use AWS Config managed rule cloudtrail-enabled (rule identifier:
  CLOUD_TRAIL_ENABLED) for continuous compliance monitoring. The rule's
  published name is cloudtrail-enabled; the rule identifier used in Config
  APIs is CLOUD_TRAIL_ENABLED. Both forms refer to the same managed rule.

SOURCE: MITRE ATT&CK® for Enterprise (Cloud) — Technique T1580
TECHNIQUE: Cloud Infrastructure Discovery
TACTIC: Discovery
ATT&CK ID: T1580
URL: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1580/
NOTE: Curated synthesis of MITRE ATT&CK wiki content and AWS IAM/EC2/STS documentation.

DESCRIPTION:
Adversaries may attempt to discover infrastructure and resources available within an
infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) environment. In AWS, this encompasses enumeration
of EC2 instances, S3 buckets, IAM roles, Lambda functions, RDS databases, and other
resources to map the attack surface before lateral movement or data collection.

RELEVANT AWS API ACTIONS:
- ec2:DescribeInstances — enumerate running EC2 instances with metadata
- ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups — map network security group rules
- ec2:DescribeVpcs / DescribeSubnets — network topology enumeration
- iam:ListRoles — enumerate IAM roles (prerequisite for trust policy analysis)
- iam:ListUsers — enumerate IAM users
- iam:GetRole / iam:GetRolePolicy — read specific role permissions
- iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy — test permissions without making actual API calls
- s3:ListAllMyBuckets — enumerate all S3 buckets in the account
- lambda:ListFunctions — enumerate Lambda functions (potential lateral movement targets)
- sts:GetCallerIdentity — determine current principal ARN and account ID (reconnaissance)

IAM-SPECIFIC RELEVANCE:
Cloud infrastructure discovery often precedes privilege escalation. An adversary with
limited initial permissions who calls iam:ListRoles, iam:GetRole, and iam:ListPolicies
is likely mapping the environment to identify escalation targets. This maps to the
reconnaissance phase before exploiting a privilege escalation path identified by
Phase 2 of this framework.
sts:GetCallerIdentity is frequently the very first action taken after credential theft.

DETECTION IN THIS FRAMEWORK:
iam:GenerateCredentialReport, iam:GetCredentialReport (T1087.004 Account Discovery) are
in the Phase 3 MITRE_SENSITIVE_ACTIONS catalog. Discovery events from the same principal
ARN as a Phase 2 source node (scp-cleared escalation path) indicate active pre-attack
reconnaissance and should trigger PARTIALLY_CORRELATED or STRONGLY_CORRELATED alerts.

REMEDIATION POINTERS:
- Apply IAM permissions boundary restricting iam:List* and iam:Get* for non-admin roles
- Enable GuardDuty monitoring for the authoritative IAM credential-exfiltration
  finding types:
    UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.InsideAWS
    UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS
  (per docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_finding-types-iam.html;
  the bare "InstanceCredentialExfiltration" string without a suffix is not a
  published GuardDuty finding type).
- Use AWS Config to alert on unusual iam:ListRoles / iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy calls
- Log all sts:GetCallerIdentity calls in CloudTrail (low cost, high signal)

It is intended for retrieval support and analyst explanation. It is not an AWS security standard and not a MITRE-authored escalation checklist.

Pattern 1: Managed policy version escalation
A principal that can create a new version of a managed policy and make that version active can change the effective permissions granted by that policy. This is operationally relevant when the policy is attached to a privileged principal.

Pattern 2: Managed policy attachment
A principal that can attach a managed policy to a role or user can change that identity’s effective permissions by adding a new managed policy.

Pattern 3: Inline policy injection
A principal that can write or replace an inline policy on a role can change the permissions directly embedded on that role.

Pattern 4: Trust policy rewrite
A principal that can update a role’s trust policy can change who is allowed to assume the role. If the modified trust policy later permits an attacker-controlled principal to call AssumeRole, the role may become reachable.

Pattern 5: Service-mediated role abuse through PassRole
A principal that can pass a powerful role to an AWS service, together with the service-specific create or configure permission, may be able to use the service as an execution path for the role’s permissions. This is especially relevant when the role trusts the service principal and the resulting workload is attacker-controlled.

Pattern 6: Instance-profile association
A principal that can add a role to an instance profile may enable EC2-based access to that role’s credentials through the instance.

Pattern 7: Group membership manipulation
A principal that can add a user to a privileged group can indirectly grant that user the permissions attached to the group.

Pattern 8: Multi-hop escalation chains
These actions may chain. For example, a principal may first rewrite a trust policy, then assume the role, then use the new permissions to attach or modify additional policies. This is operationally important for graph-based attack-path discovery.

Relationship to this framework:
Phase 2 models several of these patterns as researcher-defined graph edge types. Phase 3 correlates CloudTrail events associated with these actions against Phase 1 findings and Phase 2 paths to distinguish latent exposure from executed escalation behavior.

Framework note:
These patterns are curated implementation abstractions derived from official MITRE and AWS documentation. They should not be presented as direct MITRE procedure enumerations or as an official AWS escalation taxonomy.

Purpose:
This file provides retrieval-friendly remediation guidance for IAM misconfigurations and identity-risk findings using AWS official documentation. It is intended to support Phase 3 explanations and recommended actions.

Remediation theme: overly permissive IAM permissions
- Apply least privilege instead of broad wildcard access
- Review policies with IAM Access Analyzer policy validation
- Where possible, refine permissions using IAM Access Analyzer policy generation from CloudTrail activity
- Use permissions boundaries when delegating permissions management within an account

Remediation theme: risky policy and trust changes
- Restrict who can attach policies, create new policy versions, or update trust policies
- Review cross-account trust carefully
- Use external IDs for third-party cross-account access where appropriate to mitigate confused-deputy risk
- Continuously review public and cross-account exposure with IAM Access Analyzer

Remediation theme: long-term credentials and MFA
- Prefer temporary credentials and IAM roles over long-term access keys
- Rotate or remove long-term access keys when they are still required
- Require MFA for human users, especially privileged users
- Protect root credentials and avoid root access keys

Remediation theme: direct user policy attachment
- Prefer permission assignment through groups or roles rather than attaching policies directly to IAM users
- Review IAM users with directly attached policies and move those permissions to groups or roles when practical

Remediation theme: ABAC tag governance
- If tags are used in authorization, protect the tag model as part of the security boundary
- Restrict who may set or modify authorization-relevant tags
- Use request-tag and tag-key conditions to constrain allowed tagging operations
- Review tag-modification permissions on IAM users, roles, and target resources

Relationship to this framework:
This guidance supports Phase 3 alert explanation and remediation suggestions. It should be treated as curated AWS-based defensive guidance, not as a formal compliance baseline.
